name: Kohumono
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Cook, Thomas Louis 1969. Some tentative notes on the Kohumono language (mimeo grammar sketch, per Glottolog); no online copy found.

new_statements.quote: The transcription is broad phonetic. The prefixes listed in Tables 1 and 2 have been left unmarked for tone. Elsewhere vowels unmarked for tone have a (phonetic) mid tone. [p.120 fn.3] ... The tone of the prefixes is unpredictable, although it is mostly low. [p.122] ... Many of the tonal variations recorded are the result of a simple phonetic tone rule: M > H / __ # M, a mid tone is raised to high before another mid tone preceded by a word boundary. [p.127 fn.7]
new_statements.citation: Sterk, Jan P. 1976. The Hohumono noun class system. Journal of West African Languages 11(1-2): 119-140.
new_statements.locator: p. 120 fn. 3; p. 122 (first line); p. 127 fn. 7
new_statements.rule_in_words: No source opened says anything about word stress. The only first-hand description reachable (Sterk 1976, a noun-class study) treats Kohumono as a tone language with three phonetic levels (high, mid, low) marked on every vowel, lexically unpredictable prefix tones, tonal classes in the verb, and a phrase-level M-to-H raising rule; it makes no stress or accent statement. No claim about stress placement can be made for this language.
new_statements.exceptions: None relevant; the source notes tonal variation on nouns before determiners (p.127 fn.7) and 'tonal problems' in concord (p.133-134) but nothing about stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word and short phrase level (noun + determiner, noun phrases, short clauses) in elicited examples from Bahumono students at the University of Calabar; the tone rule is stated across a word boundary. Not a phonology section: the tone remarks are footnotes to a noun-class study. The phonological sketch proper is Cook 1969, which could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Sterk 1976 calls the language 'Hohumono' (speakers at the University of Calabar, Bahumono people of Ediba/Obubra); same languoid as Glottolog kohu1244 / ISO bcs (Glottolog maps 'Hohumono' to Kohumono [bcs] in the Blench 2014 record). No dialect is specified.

sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent. Only a transcription footnote and tone notes: broad phonetic transcription, unmarked vowels have phonetic mid tone (p.120 fn.3); prefix tone unpredictable, mostly low (p.122); phonetic rule M > H / __ # M (p.127 fn.7); several tonal classes in the verb system (p.134). Three phonetic tone levels (H, M, L) marked throughout; vowel harmony (ATR).
